content.title: How long is a trip to the moon with our current technology?
content.text: The Apollo missions used a near minimum energy trajectory to the moon, a trajectory in which the spacecraft outbound from Earth slowed almost to a stop before falling toward the moon, then slowed again on the way back, before falling toward the Earth.This orbit takes about three days each way. If you want to burn more fuel, you can get to the moon much faster, but it would take a LOT more fuel—more to burn on the way out, more to slow down once you get there, and more to move all the extra fuel you have to bring along. No one is likely to do that, at least not with any sort of chemical rocket. Fuel is heavy, and it’s much, much, much cheaper to carry a few extra pounds of oxygen, CO2 scrubbers, and shrimp cocktail than to go faster and launch tens of thousands more pounds of fuel.If you’re interested in space travel, you might enjoy my free award-winning scifi sampler.How long would it take to reach the Moon for a landing using today's technology, compared with 1969?I’m not quite sure whether you’re asking about the time from launch to landing - or the time from start of rocket-development to first mission…so I guess I’ll answer both. TIME FROM LAUNCH TO LANDING: The actual transit time would likely be exactly the same as in the Apollo era…a few days. The thing is that the speed a spacecraft has to move at to remain in a stable orbit is unchanging. Technology can’t alter that. So as you go from a stable orbit around Earth to a stable orbit around the Moon - your start and end speeds are the same as they were for Apollo - and the “trans-lunar-injection” phase is going to be more or less the same speed too. So - yeah - about the same as for Apollo…and that’s unlikely to get much faster because there really isn’t a need to go any faster. TIME FROM START OF DEVELOPMENT TO FIRST MISSION: From Kennedy’s speech that officially started the Apollo project to the first landing was about 8 years. But that’s kinda cheating because NASA had been gradually working towards this goal for at least 10 years beforehand. These days, we already have rockets that could propel a suitable payload to the Moon. The SLS rocket is way behind schedule - and is a very costly program - which I very much doubt will survive for long into the next US presidential term without cancellation. However, the SpaceX Falcon Heavy could launch about 25 tonnes to the Moon if it’s rockets were expended. The Apollo command module weighed about 5.6 tonnes, the service module weighed 23 tonnes and the Lunar module about 15 tonnes. So you couldn’t do this in one go. But with modern computer technology - it would be rather easy to launch the Lunar module by itself and have it wait in a lunar orbit - then when it’s known that it’s all ready to go - launch the command and service modules a few days later on a second rocket. Rendezvous in Moon orbit - transfer crew into the Lunar module and we’re good to go. So the launch part would require no new designs at all. The “Service Module” could be replaced by the Crew Dragon - using the extended version that NASA have ordered for 2024 that’s designed to be launched on a Falcon Heavy. So the remaining issues are to design the new Lunar module. It’s harder to say how long that would take - but NASA have several contracts out there for a 2024 mission. All of this is actually what NASA are doing with the Artemis project - which is intended to return astronauts to the moon in 2024. Another route entirely would to give the job to SpaceX’s up-coming StarShip (which is kinda what’s happening in a parallel contract from NASA). StarShip would simply launch from Earth - go directly to the Moon and land the entire StarShip there. With a 100 tonne payload and a crew complement of up to 100 people - this craft would be easily capable of the trip. However, it’s not QUITE that simple because the StarShip wasn’t really designed for Moon landings. When StarShip lands on Earth or Mars - it has to use those winglets and do some aerobraking on the way down - ending with a propulsive touchdown. For the Moon, there can be no aerobreaking - and full propulsive landings would run the risk of wrecking the lunar surface that the spacecraft needs...How long would it take to reach the Moon for a landing using today's technology, compared with 1969?Apollo 11 took just shy of 76 hours to reach lunar orbit. Apollo 17 took 86 hours. The others were in between. The time varies depending on where the Moon is at the time and where on the Moon we wish to visit. The first Artemis mission is currently designed to take 103 hours to reach lunar orbit. While technology has evolved, two things haven’t: physics and the desire to use payload mass for things other than propellants. A lunar trajectory is designed such that there is a burn conducted to accelerate the vehicle into an intercept trajectory. Once upon that trajectory, the vehicle coasts and decelerates. We want the vehicle to decelerate such that when it reaches the Moon, the difference between the Moon’s velocity and the vehicle’s velocity is as small as possible, because any difference has to be dealt with by firing thrusters and burning more fuel. Yes, using propellants to decelerate the vehicle would allow us to reduce the travel time, but every ounce or gram of propellant would take the place of an ounce or gram of payload - mission hardware, experiments, instruments, batteries, the crew themselves.How were we able to put a man on the moon with the level of technology that was available in 1969? Did NASA have advanced technologies that were just not made public?In 2010, my 14-year-old son asked me a similar question. I had a smartphone, an iPad, every member (5) in my home had a laptop and we had five flat TVs. Of course we had a good Wifi, cable TV, etc. I had told him before many things about ‘60s and ‘70s. At the beginning of the ‘70s we had only one TV in my family (of course black and white), in Spain we only had two TV channels, of course, we didn’t have computers, mobiles, etc. But after listening to his question, I told him one thing that made him frown. When I was a kid, we could travel between Paris and New York in three hours and a half (if you had enough money to buy a ticket). You could take a Concorde at 9am in Paris and you could land in New York at 6:30 am local time, with a flight time duration of 3.30 hours. Today, if you want to fly to New York from Paris, the average duration of your flight would be 7.30 hours. Then I told him that the Concorde was designed in the 50s and 60s and her first flight was in March 1969. Here you can see a photo of this first flight:So in the XX century, there was a plane which needed less time to fly from Europe to America than another one in the XXI (at least until now). Then I showed him another airplanes that were designed in the ‘50s and ‘60s and began to fly in ‘60s-’70s: 1.- A Boeing 747 the biggest airplane in history (passengers of course) until the arrival of Airbus A380:2.- An outstanding Blackbird; one of the fastest airplanes in history:3.- The Grumman F14:And Finally the superb Saturn V rocket -- the most powerful in history until the SLS begins to fly in the following years.So in the 1960s aeronautics and space engineering lived their golden era. Why? Because NASA had something more important than technology: political will and a lot of money to spend. If the same effort would have been maintained for 50 years, we would have had a Lunar Base, and another one in Mars already.Ask a pro: "I'm 65 with $1M saved. What's my retirement budget?"This quiz matches nearly 50,000 people each month with vetted financial advisors.Only Ernie Dunbar actually answered the question. The “technology” will be the same today it was in 1969 - free return trajectory; which will take the same amount of time as it did 48 years ago. It is also the safest and the method, I assume, we will use when we return. It is the most fuel efficient and provides an emergency route home without requiring a burn, other than course corrections. Of course the “technology” mentioned here only applies to the mechanics of the flight path. Obviously computing power has advanced by magnitudes. I think the questioner was confusing the term as regards to the flight path and the time required. BTW, the Apollo 11 crew and all those who followed did not “slow almost to a stop” as the first answer stated. That’s not how a “free return trajectory” works. I’ll leave it to others more well versed than I in orbital mechanics, to elaborate this point.How long would it take to reach the Moon for a landing using today's technology, compared with 1969?I am only a Theoretical Physicist and not an Astronaut (though I did work for NASA in my younger years), but I believe I can offer the following with a better than 95% certainty: The flight requirements are all still the same: 1. Launch from Earth presumably to an TOI (Terra Orbital Insertion) — NO, one can NOT just launch off of Mother Earth and go to the Moon;2. Fire a significant amount of fuel to exit Earth Orbit and enter a TTLT (Trans Terra-Lunar Trajectory) that would take a capsule (maned or not) towards the position the Moon will be when the capsule arrives — NO, one cannot just drive over to the moon — it is a significant “RRP” (Running Rendezvous Problem);3. Burn more fuel for LOI (Lunar Orbital Insertion);4. Burn more fuel on some form of a Lunar Lander to escape Lunar orbit and head down to the Lunar surface leaving the Command Module in orbit;5. Burn more fuel to “fly” down to the surface, choose a landing spot, & execute a landing of a LEM (Lunar Excursion Module). Then of course, I would hope we would like to bring any on-board Astronauts back home to Earth — it’s not much of a party if we leave the hero’s there! You need to do several launches to achieve this, but we have a number of rockets on the ground in various stages We need a craft capable of landing on the moon. It looks like the Soyuz could do that. We have Soyuz up there attached to the ISS, so we don’t even have to lift another one up. We need a rocket big enough to move a Soyuz from LEO to Lunar orbit and execute a deorbit burn. A top stage of any of the various craft we are using to resupply the ISS should do that; launch it with no payload, so that you’ve got sufficient fuel to get the top stage itself to the ISS. Then move fuel up, sufficient to refuel that top stage. Now the hard part, moving fuel from your resupply into your top stage. This may require some engineering solutions. Then you have to tie the Soyuz onto the rocket. But you don’t have to do a pretty job, because you aren’t going to go into an atmosphere. The two things you need to achieve are A) it has to stay mounted and not wiggle around during burns and B) you have to be able to drop it once it’s done pushing the Soyuz around. Calculate two burns, the first gets you up out of LEO and into a Lunar intercept course, where you go from being more attracted to Earth to being more attracted to the Moon. There’s no need to go into lunar orbit, because you’re not leaving a command capsule behind. The second burn is to slow the fall down once you’re pretty close to the moon. Then you drop the rocket and you’re just in the Soyuz, falling slowly towards the surface, but of course accelerating due to Moon gravity. The Soyuz, though, is designed to land on land. It uses parachutes, which won’t do any good, but it also uses rockets both for deorbit burn and for a soft landing. Given that lunar gravity is 1/6th that of Earth, this should suffice to get to a soft touchdown. Now, we do have one slight problem. We’ve got live astronauts/cosmonauts on the surface of the moon, which was the goal. It was a one way trip. The Soyuz TMA-M has life support for 30 person-days. Figure 3 days to reach the Moon, and if you only put one person in there, they have 27 days to live. But that means bottled up in the craft. Walking around on the surface requires a suit and supplies, and there will also be some losses due to airlock passage. I’m not sure what the purpose of this trip was, so I went with the minimum that would meet the criteria given. The Apollo missions landed a craft which could not only land on the Moon, but also get back up to Lunar orbit, and they put a craft in place there in lunar orbit which could get the crew back to Earth orbit, and then deorbit and make it all the way down to a splash landing. That would be a lot harder, and take a lot longer.That depends, will we be lazy and rely on 1950’s methods of reaching lunar orbit or, will we put some of our cutting edge technology to the test pushing further, faster, driving to develop and use some truly next generation propulsion technology? What took us the better part of three days, ( Drifting ), to reach the moon, should today be less than 12 hours, ( under point to point rapid transit. ) No excuses! We have some real world 2020 technology and we can do this! We have several good reasons for returning to the moon. One of the most profound reasons is to inspire future generations of space explorers to reach for the stars and do it ever further, faster and drive us ever closer to the discoveries that will give human kind the opportunities to build a better and brighter future for all of us! The headlines that will hold the greatest inspiration will read something like this… “ The Eagle has returned to the moon in record time!.. 10 hours 27 minutes, 17 seconds! Next stop, Mars!” Concept: ( R.T.A.P.S. ), Rapid Transit Assist Propulsion system. A direct thrust reversal nacelle based vehicle attachment designed to quickly hook up / detach to various platforms including, star ships, probes, supply crates, rescue pods and could also be use to move the I.S.S. from earth orbit to lunar orbit and vice versa. Envisioned this while watching tugs help guide and move ships safely in and out of harbor , imagining tug like vehicles that could rapidly assist vehicle in space on dedicated routes from Earth to the moon and back again. More advanced versions would go to Mars and back. This system of rapid transit assist would be used to travel to destinations within the inner solar system. Example: The R Taps vehicle would quickly attach to a star ship and safely guide it to lunar orbit then detach and remain in orbit until needed for the return trip home or for an extended journey to another destination, (Mars). An R Taps vehicle would be a re-usable, cost effective way of improving travel times for a multitude of craft. A small station of R Taps vehicles could be placed in Earth, Lunar and Mars orbit to be called upon when needed.How were we able to put a man on the moon with the level of technology that was available in 1969? Did NASA have advanced technologies that were just not made public?One thing that we must realize is that the Apollo program was primarily an engineering program. Very few scientific discoveries were required. Isaac Newton taught us all of the physics we needed to know to get to the moon and back. The calculus necessary to calculate the trajectory of a rocket that is accelerating while rapidly losing mass is complicated, but still pretty much what Newton taught us. Nearly every time you hear a question in the form of, “If we can send men to the moon why can’t we…” the ellipses (…) is filled in with a required invention. Curing cancer, or the common cold or achieving world peace are far more difficult. GPS technology is also more difficult since it requires the relativity that Einstein taught us in addition to the physics of motion. The major invention of the Apollo program was the silicon chip that allowed a rudimentary computer small enough to send into space. That was a huge invention from which we are still reaping benefits. The standard computers of that time literally filled up a room. (I worked with one of them until 1992. When it was retired, the memory cards were put on display. An 8 KB card was about 8 x 10 inches. With a 10X loupe, you could see the individual ferrite collar bits.)The other major factor was, as C. Stuart Hardwick stated, “spending a crap ton of money over ten years.” We also marshaled our best and brightest engineers and scientists for the task. I remember going with my parents to a PTA meeting at our grade school where a neighbor asked if we had the facilities to teach our children the science we need to beat the Russians to the moon. Beating the Russians to the moon in the 1960s was just as important as defeating Hitler in the 1940s. Edit: Thanks for the upvotes. The following started as a reply to a comment. I’m not sure I would agree we were more risk-tolerant in those days. We were definitely less risk-aware. I used to work with some people who had been part of the Apollo mission planning process. If you are familiar with Gantt charts, they produced what was then certainly the world's largest Gantt chart. (It may still be one of the world's largest.) They had a companion Potential Problem Analysis chart along with it (similar to today's Failure Mode Effects Analysis (FMEA) charts). They looked at every single part of the mission and asked what could go wrong and considered ways to mitigate the risk. They had backup systems for somewhere between 97% and 98% of the process. If you look at the overall record of the space program up through Apollo, it tracks with that kind of safety record. There was one fatal incident with three fatalities. There were three other incidents that could have produced fatalities: Gus Grissom’s Mercury flight, Gemini 8, and Apollo 13. This is another example of a massive engineering project that employed an existing methodology on a massive scale rather than inventing new things. I believed they prepared for everything they could think of, but they had a failure of imagination that led to the Apollo fire.How were we able to put a man on the moon with the level of technology that was available in 1969? Did NASA have advanced technologies that were just not made public?Q: How were we able to put a man on the moon with the level of technology that was available in 1969?By spending a crap ton of money over ten years, peaking at 5% of the federal budget. And by relying as much as possible on already proven technology, which isn’t as “high-tech” as you think (more on that below).Q: Did NASA have advanced technologies that were just not made public?Not really. They developed the advanced technologies they needed, and except where they were borrowing from the military, they then made them public. NASA’s primary job, after all, is to promote and nurture the American aerospace industry. Here are a few examples of how the technology came to be:Back in 1961, NASA knew it would need a big moon rocket, but they didn’t know how big or have a design for it. They knew, however, that back in 1955, Rocketdyne had started work on the granddaddy of rocket engines for the Air Force. The first attempt (the E-1) had been a dead end, but the second try (the F-1) had been successfully fired in 1957—the year before NASA was founded. The Air Force had abandoned the engine, but NASA paid Rocketdyne to continue development, and the engine was improved continually throughout the Apollo program, including thrust and reliability upgrades from one mission to another. For all that, the F-1 was in many ways a crude engine by today’s standards. In particular, it required hundreds of difficult, manual welds in refractory metal, all of which had to be perfect. Today, the same engine could be formed in three (principle) pieces and welded together by robots, but back then, it was all done by hand.NASA knew the big moon rocket would need an utterly reliable navigation system—though they didn’t know how good it really needed to be. They also knew it would need a more flexible computer than missiles of the time, or the crew would be overwhelmed. The MIT Instrumentation Laboratory had been involved in both fields for the military, so it was the obvious choice to design the IMU, Computer, and navigational sensors. Companies like Raytheon, who had built earlier systems for the military, were the obvious people to build it. It turned out that radio ranging from Earth was about as accurate as the Apollo navigation system, but the crew were happy to have the backup. Again, this bleeding edge 1969 technology is mickey mouse today. A modern laser ring gyroscope is more accurate, less power hungry, and a damn site lighter than the Apollo IMU, and my cell phone has 100,000 times the power of the 70 pound, 55 watt AGC. NASA did, however, buy integrated circuits as fast as Fairchild Semiconductor could make them, spurring development in the field, and they had to learn to build human-rated systems for the radiation filled space environment and keep them cool in a cabin that had no air convection (and sometimes no air), and we still use those lessons today.Since the new moon rocket was going to take a while (whether the Nova or the Saturn), Werner Von Braun’s team assembled a Frankenstein’s Erector Set of spare parts from Juno, Jupiter, and other earlier rockets, and while bizarre and not very efficient, the resultant “Saturn I” served Apollo’s needs in low Earth orbit through the Skylab era.When Boeing finally started on the Saturn, they found that the first stage required aluminum welds longer than anyone in the world knew how to make. So they figured it out. Today, we can weld nuclear submarine hulls that are inches thick and 100 feet around. That’s technology.When North American Aviation was given the contract for the Saturn second stage (The S-II) they didn’t have enough weight budget for the normal bulkheads and insulation between the liquid oxygen and hydrogen tanks. They came up with an insulating common bulkhead made of fiberglass and phenolic resin. When they had trouble getting the (then cutting edge) epoxy adhesives to perform, they called on local surf board makers who were happy to share their expertise (That might have been the S-IVB upper stage, built by Douglas).To study propellant behavior in large booster stages, NASA borrowed ten-year old technology from early spy satellites and used ejectable pods to recover film cameras mounted inside the tanks of test flights.To save power, the Command Module was primarily lit by bespoke compact fluorescent floodlights, made by GE using technology already under development, and later refined into the (now essentially obsolete) CFL.LEM design started in 1962 with a request for proposals to 11 firms. As development of the rest of the mission components proceeded, however, every limitation or compromise ate into the allowable weight for the LEM. Later improvements in engine thrust and operational efficiency opened that up and enabled the heavier, later missions, but when Grumman won the contract, the weight restrictions seemed impossible to meet. So they ditched the chairs (who need’s ‘em?) and the windows (portals will do, if facing just right). They held company-wide contests to shave weight off the design. For the pressure hull/fuselage, they machined solid sheets of aircraft aluminum into grids, then chemically etched the remaining metal to create tapered panels, barely thicker than a soda can in some places, but sufficient to hold the mere 5 psi atmosphere within the LEM. It worked and met NASA’s requirements, but it cost a fortune, and each LEM was rated for only a few pressurization cycles. Today, we could build the ascent stage for half the weight and 100 times the life using carbon fiber composites, and cut the descent stage (dry) weight by about 80%.Large booster stages could rely on acceleration (either from the main engines or small “ullage motors”) to keep propellants flowing, but that wouldn’t work for true spacecraft, which needed to be able to fire thrusters at will, both for ullage and maneuvering, and as a backup in case of main engine failure. NASA’s solution was to use rubber bladders like those used in WWII aircraft to prevent fuel tanks from exploding when hit by enemy fire. Helium, pressing between the bladder and the intake, kept the propellant where it needed to be. You sometimes hear people talking about how the Apollo ascent engine couldn’t be tested because the hypergolic propellants would have corroded it before launch. That’s not true. The engine (and thrusters) could easily be made to resist corrosion, but the rubber bladders couldn’t. When the space shuttle came along, NASA spent a lot of money inventing an alternative that relies on surface tension and operational restrictions to eliminate the need for the bladder (or a more complex alternative), and that’s why the shuttle’s OMS engines and thrusters didn’t have to be replaced after every flight.The main heat shield for the first 6 Mercury flights was a single piece of machined beryllium—a technology lifted from early ICBMs. Mercury and Gemini capsules were protected from reentry heating by high temperature alloy shingles developed from the same nuclear missile research. Later Mercury and Gemini flights used a brand new ablative material developed specially for them, and this was refined to protect the whole Apollo Command Module and dispense with the metal shingles. The heat shield for the leading edges of the space shuttle was derived from research into the ablative shields used on Apollo. The ablative heat shield used by the modern Orion, Space-x and Boeing capsules was developed from that used on Apollo, but modified to essentially decompose into the same pyrolyzed carbon that protected the leading edges of the shuttle, creating a reusable, self-renewing heat shield.By the way. NASA wasn’t created to send people to the moon. It was created to assist American aerospace businesses and, in matters of aeronautical or space, the American public and all mankind. The reason we could build a LEM of composites today…the reason Boeing can build a jumbo jet of composites today—is in part because NASA paid to have those materials characterized so they could use them on the payload bay doors of the shuttle. And the reason today’s space entrepreneurs can show off their fancy propulsive landing systems is—in large part—because NASA paid a lot of money to essentially create the practice of Computational Fluid Dynamics, without which neither the shuttle nor these modern wonders could have flown. We went to the moon with what was, at the time, cutting edge, custom-made, sometimes poorly understood, often barely adequate technology. The basic science hasn’t changed much since, but our manufacturing ability has grown by leaps and bounds—in part due to the spur it received from Apollo and the last fifty years of refinement. I said above that the technology that took us to the moon isn’t as advanced as you might think. I mentioned carbon composites and robotic welders and the heavy inertial platform and computer, and the WWII rubber bladders. Apollo also used parabolic dish antennas, both in space and on the ground, though newer ground antennas typically use the more efficient offset Gregorian configuration and spacecraft now often use fractal antennas—which were originally designed for cell phones.[Apollo CSM with quad parabolic high gain antenna by engine and simitar VHF antenna (white) mid-way between and behind thruster quads.] [Offset Gregorian radio telescope.]How long would it take to reach the Moon for a landing using today's technology, compared with 1969?About the same amount of time. Technology has nothing to do with how fast we get there. The Saturn IVB booster performed the translunar injection burn used by the Apollo spacecraft. It boosted the velocity of the spacecraft to the point where it would get it most of the way there until it was actually grabbed by the moon's gravity and pulled the rest of the way in. they did it that way because it was and still is the most fuel efficient and weight efficient way to do it. They could absolutely have built a much bigger booster and just blasted their way to the moon but then they would have had to have had another large booster to be able to slow them down and eliminate all of that excess velocity once they got there. That would of course required an even larger booster to perform the TLI and would have required an even larger launch vehicle than the Saturn V to get them off the ground. There really is no reason to get there faster. 3 days is nothing.How long is a trip to the moon with our current technology? The fastest object so far to leave Earth was “New Horizons” Pluto probe launched in 2006. It crossed Moon’s orbit after 9 hours. So if you just wanted to hit the Moon and make a new crater, it could be done that fast. But not if you want to land or to get into orbit. You want to approach as slowly as possible. If human passengers are involved, you probably do same thing Apollo did — go on an elliptical orbit, tangent to Moon’s orbit at the apogee. That gets you to the Moon in three days. With unmanned probes you do not have to worry about food, oxygen and bone loss, and can go much slower. A private lander by Intuitive Machines was launched yesterday; it will reach the Moon after about a week:https://www.reuters.com/science/intuitive-machines-set-embark-second-moon-landing-mission-2025-02-26/And one lander spent 14 months spiraling out to the Moon. Unless there is an overriding reason for it, you do not want to go fast.About the same amount of time as it took 60 years ago… 72 hours from launch to lunar landing. Technology cannot alter orbital mechanics. It can only make today’s spacecraft safer, more reliable, and simpler to operate. The exception would be if the technology was ultra-radical or something… like say we found a new type of super dense fuel that would make the need for fuel conservation unnecessary… basically an unlimited fuel supply. In that scenario, you could just keep burning your engines as you accelerate faster and faster. The less curvature the spacecraft’s trajectory has enroute to the moon, the less distance it has to cover, since the shortest distance between two points is always a straight line. What causes the curved flight path is the gravitational pull of the Earth, moon, and sun… and a completely straight line of travel is not possible. If you had unlimited or huge amounts of fuel, however, you could keep burning and make your trajectory “less curvy”…and you could cut the time to the moon (and back to Earth) very significantly. Luna 1 made the journey in 34 hours. The size and mass of the spacecraft, and the particular orbit sizes you’re aiming to achieve will change travel time somewhat, but not significantly. With the Apollo missions, it took a crew of 3, and constant support of Mission Control and hundreds of people on Earth. It would be possible today for a single individual to make the trip, with limited support from MC. First of all, most of the spacecraft’s systems can be automated and monitored by computer. And there would be a backup piece of hardware for every primary piece… such as 2 flight management computers, 2 environmental control computers, 2 laser gyros, better radars, even triple redundancy sometimes. Apollo had a single primitive computer, single mechanical gyro susceptible to errors, and though it had a few automated systems, most things had to be operated manually. That alone requires an additional astronaut, like older airplanes required a flight engineer.
